# R Lab: Basic Operations of R Programming

#Part A — Creating Data Frames

#Question #1
```{r}
# Part a: create the data frame and save it as shoesize.csv
ShoeSize <- c(6.5, 9.0, 8.5, 8.5, 10.5, 7.0, 9.5, 9.0, 13.0, 7.5, 10.5, 8.5, 12.0, 10.5,
              13.0, 11.5, 8.5, 5.0, 10.0, 6.5, 7.5, 8.5, 10.5, 8.5, 10.5, 11.0, 9.0, 13.0)
Height <- c(66.0, 68.0, 64.5, 65.0, 70.0, 64.0, 70.0, 71.0, 72.0, 64.0, 74.5, 67.0, 71.0, 71.0,
            77.0, 72.0, 59.0, 62.0, 72.0, 66.0, 64.0, 67.0, 73.0, 69.0, 72.0, 70.0, 69.0, 70.0)
Gender <- c("F", "F", "F", "F", "M", "F", "F", "F", "M", "F", "M", "F", "M", "M",
            "M", "M", "F", "F", "M", "F", "F", "M", "M", "F", "M", "M", "M", "M")

shoes_df <- data.frame(ShoeSize = ShoeSize, Height = Height, Gender = Gender)
write.csv(shoes_df, "shoesize.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
# Part b: import the saved csv and display the last 5 rows
shoes <- read.csv("shoesize.csv")
tail(shoes, 5)
```

```{r}
# Part c: structure and content
str(shoes)
head(shoes)
```

```{r}
# Part d: dimensions
dim(shoes)
nrow(shoes)
ncol(shoes)
```

```{r}
# Part e: summary vs str
summary(shoes)

# Answer: str() shows the structure, like the data type of each column and a
# preview of the values. summary() shows statistics, like the min, median, mean,
# and max for the numeric columns. For Gender it only shows the length and class
# because it is text.
```

```{r}
# Part f: subsets of males and females with shoe size and height
males <- shoes[shoes$Gender == "M", c("ShoeSize", "Height")]
females <- shoes[shoes$Gender == "F", c("ShoeSize", "Height")]
males
females

# Answer: There are 14 males and 14 females. The males mostly have bigger shoe
# sizes and are taller than the females.
```

```{r}
# Part g: mean of shoe size and height
mean(shoes$ShoeSize)
mean(shoes$Height)

# Answer: The mean shoe size is about 9.41 and the mean height is about
# 68.57.
```

```{r}
# Part h: relationship between shoe size and height
cor(shoes$ShoeSize, shoes$Height)

# Answer: Yes, there is a positive relationship. People with bigger shoe sizes
# are usually taller, and the correlation is about 0.78, which is fairly
# strong. This makes sense because taller people usually have bigger feet.
```

#Question #2
```{r}
gender_f <- factor(shoes$Gender, levels = c("F", "M"),
                   labels = c("Female", "Male"))
gender_f
table(gender_f)
levels(gender_f)

# Answer: Gender is a nominal variable because Female and Male are just
# categories, and one is not worth more than the other. So I made it a factor
# with two levels, Female and Male.
```

#Question #3
```{r}
# Answer: Knitting always uses the folder of the Rmd file as the working
# directory, so R looks for shoesize.csv in the same place every time. If it
# used whatever folder my console was in, the file might not be found on
# another computer. This way, when I share the Rmd and the csv together, it
# runs the same for the other person.
```

#Question #4
```{r}
str(shoes)

# Answer: R made Gender a chr (character) column, which is what I expected
# because it contains the letters F and M. ShoeSize and Height are numeric.
# If ShoeSize was imported as character because of a stray value like a
# typo or a letter in the file, then mean() and cor() would not work or give
# NA or errors, and sorting would be wrong because text sorts alphabetically
# (for example, 10.5 would come before 9.0).
```

#Question #5
```{r}
head(shoes)
tail(shoes)

# Answer: head() only shows the beginning of the file, so a problem at the
# end would be missed. tail() checks the end. For example, extra blank rows,
# a notes or total row at the bottom, or incomplete rows would only show up
# with tail(). Checking both makes sure the whole file was imported properly.
```

#Question #6
```{r}
# Part a: correlation across all observations
cor(shoes$ShoeSize, shoes$Height)
```

```{r}
# Part b: all rows where ShoeSize is greater than or equal to 11
shoes[shoes$ShoeSize >= 11, ]
```

#Question #7
```{r}
mean(females$Height)
mean(males$Height)
mean(females$ShoeSize)
mean(males$ShoeSize)

# Answer: The females have a mean height of about 65.68 and a mean shoe size
# of about 7.86, while the males have a mean height of about 71.46 and a mean
# shoe size of about 10.96. So the males are taller and have bigger shoes on
# average. The dataset supports a relationship between shoe size and height,
# but gender is also an important factor, because part of the overall
# correlation may come from the males being both taller and having bigger
# shoes. So I should check the relationship separately for each gender.
```
